input: Set these variables: APP_NAME='myservice', APP_PORT=8080, DB_HOST='db.prod.internal', DB_PORT=5432, LOG_LEVEL='warn'. Then use a heredoc (cat <<EOF) to generate /etc/app/config.yaml with these variables interpolated into a YAML structure with sections 'app:' (name, port), 'database:' (host, port), and 'logging:' (level). Print the generated file contents.

transcript.final_response:
I set the variables, created `/etc/app`, and used an unquoted heredoc (`cat <<EOF`) to write `/etc/app/config.yaml`. Because `EOF` isn't quoted, the shell filled in each `${VAR}` with its value. Here's the generated file:

```yaml
app:
  name: myservice
  port: 8080
database:
  host: db.prod.internal
  port: 5432
logging:
  level: warn
```

The command I ran:

```bash
APP_NAME='myservice'; APP_PORT=8080; DB_HOST='db.prod.internal'; DB_PORT=5432; LOG_LEVEL='warn'
mkdir -p /etc/app
cat <<EOF > /etc/app/config.yaml
app:
  name: ${APP_NAME}
  port: ${APP_PORT}
database:
  host: ${DB_HOST}
  port: ${DB_PORT}
logging:
  level: ${LOG_LEVEL}
EOF
cat /etc/app/config.yaml
```

If you write the delimiter as `<<'EOF'` with quotes, the shell won't fill in the variables and the file will contain the literal `${APP_NAME}` text.
